system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2152-08-17 20:57:00 to 2152-08-23 20:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, kidney transplant, and peripheral artery disease was admitted for management of non-healing ulcers on his right foot. He underwent balloon angioplasty of the right anterior tibial artery to improve blood flow, which was successful as evidenced by the return of a palpable dorsalis pedis pulse. The procedure used minimal contrast to protect kidney function, and his renal values remained stable. He was started on clopidogrel for 30 days and advised to hold chlorthalidone until nephrology follow-up. He recovered well, with stable vital signs and pain control, and was discharged home with instructions for wound care, activity restrictions, and follow-up appointments with nephrology and vascular surgery.
problems: Atherosclerosis of native arteries of right leg with ulceration of other part of foot
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with foot ulcer
Non-pressure chronic ulcer of other part of right foot with unspecified severity
Peripheral vascular angioplasty status with implants and grafts
Acquired absence of other right toe(s)
Acquired absence of right great toe

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male ___ DM, diabetic nephropathy s/p renal
transplant x 2 (___) and PAD with femoral bypass and stenting with left
lower extremity ulcer by dermatology with path c/w calciphylaxis.// please
place single lumen chest port and leave accessed- Blanch aware

COMPARISON:  None

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___,
performed the procedure.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
50 mcg of fentanyl and  mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 20 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl and Versed for moderate sedation as above, 1% local
lidocaine,,
CONTRAST: 0 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  0.3 min, 5 mGy

PROCEDURE
1. Right internal jugular approach chest single lumen Port-a-cath placement

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the explanation of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The upper chest was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.
Under continuous ultrasound guidance, the right internal jugular vein was
noted to have partially occlusive thrombus, but accessed using a micropuncture
needle. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after intravenous
access, which confirmed vein patency. Subsequently a Nitinol wire was passed
into the right atrium using fluoroscopic guidance. The needle was exchanged
for a micropuncture sheath. The Nitinol wire was removed and a short ___
wire was advanced to make appropriate measurements for catheter length. The
___ wire was then passed distally into the IVC.
Next, attention was turned towards creation of a subcutaneous pocket over the
upper anterior chest wall. After instilling superficial and deeper local
anesthesia using lidocaine mixed with epinephrine, a 2.5 cm transverse
incision was made and a subcutaneous pocket was created by using blunt
dissection. The single lumen port was then connected to the catheter.  The
catheter was tunneled from the subcutaneous pocket towards the venotomy site
from where it was brought out using a tunneling device. The port was then
connected to the catheter and checks were made for any leakage by accessing
the diaphragm using a non-coring ___ needle. No leaks were found.
The port was then placed in the subcutaneous pocket and secured with ___
ethilon sutures on either side. The venotomy tract was dilated using the
introducer of the peel-away sheath supplied. Following this, the peel-away
sheath was placed over the ___ wire through which the port was threaded into
the right side of the heart with the tip in the right atrium.  The sheath was
then peeled away.
The subcutaneous pocket was closed in layers with ___ interrupted and ___
subcuticular continuous Vicryl sutures.  Steri-strips were used to close the
venotomy incision site. Steri-Strips were applied over the sutures. Final spot
fluoroscopic image demonstrating good alignment of the catheter and no
kinking. The tip is in the right atrium.
The port was accessed using a non coring ___ needle and could be aspirated
and flushed easily. Sterile dressings were applied. The patient tolerated the
procedure well without immediate complication.  The port was  left accessed as
requested.

FINDINGS: 

Partially occlusive thrombus in the right internal jugular vein.  Final
fluoroscopic image showing port with catheter tip terminating in the right
atrium.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a single lumen chest power Port-a-cath via the right
internal jugular venous approach. The tip of the catheter terminates in the
right atrium. The catheter is ready for use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with chills this morning after a skin biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I was fine until 4 a.m. I had shaking chills and checked my temperature at home—it was 99.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the biopsy was on that ulcer on your left leg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the dermatologist did it yesterday. It’s been getting worse for months. Now it’s really painful and has this black scab on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed the dermatology note. They were concerned it might be calciphylaxis, which is a rare condition related to calcium buildup in small blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Calciphylaxis? I’ve never heard of that. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be. It often happens in patients with kidney disease. The good news is we’re starting to get answers, and we’ll treat it aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried it was an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We thought so too. Your white blood cell count is a bit high, so we started antibiotics just in case—cefepime and vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on those long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait for the biopsy results. If it confirms calciphylaxis and no infection, we’ll stop the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The pathology report came back. It confirms calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the blood and urine cultures were negative. The fever and chills were likely a reaction to the biopsy in the setting of this condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s the treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start sodium thiosulfate, which helps dissolve calcium deposits. It’s given through an IV, so we’ll need a port.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A port? Like for chemotherapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, similar. It’ll make getting the IV medication easier over the next few months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Typically three months, but we’ll adjust based on how you respond. The dermatology team will manage that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling the port placement for tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a big procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s minor. Done under sedation. A small device goes under the skin in your chest, with a catheter going into a vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get pain meds. Most patients tolerate it well. You’ll be back in your room within a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The port was placed successfully this morning. The catheter tip is in the right atrium, and it’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel it. I woke up and it was done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll start the first dose of sodium thiosulfate tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop them after today since there’s no infection. Your fever has resolved, and labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started the sodium thiosulfate this morning. We’ll give it three times a week, and increase the dose as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rarely, it can affect heart rhythm. We checked your EKG before starting—your QTc was 452, which is safe. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my kidney numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 1.8 on admission, a bit high from your baseline of 1.5. But it’s coming down to 1.7—likely from dehydration. We’ll keep you hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? My sugars have been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing your insulin here. You’ll go home on the same regimen. Your A1c is still high at 10.6, so we’ll need to work on that with your endocrinologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve made some medication changes. We stopped your vitamin D and started cinacalcet to help control calcium levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why stop vitamin D?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In calciphylaxis, vitamin D can worsen calcium buildup. Cinacalcet helps regulate it. We’ll check your calcium and PTH in four weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was high when you arrived—over 200. But it’s been stable on your usual meds: labetalol, nifedipine, spironolactone, and doxazosin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your meds, especially tacrolimus, leflunomide, and the new cinacalcet. Take acetaminophen and oxycodone for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the port?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sodium thiosulfate three times a week at the infusion clinic. The port must be flushed with heparin if not used for a few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See dermatology and transplant nephrology. Get labs in four weeks—CBC, BMP, calcium, PTH. And never take warfarin—it can worsen calciphylaxis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure my other doctors know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll send them all the details. You’re doing well—keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—can I use the collagenase ointment on the leg ulcer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not on that ulcer. It’s for other wounds only. The dermatology team recommended Vaseline, xeroform, and daily dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will go over discharge instructions and your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Stay on top of your appointments and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be watching your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you then.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with a history of type 2 diabetes, kidney transplant, and peripheral artery disease was admitted for evaluation of shaking chills following a punch biopsy of a chronic left lower leg ulcer. The biopsy confirmed calciphylaxis, explaining his symptoms. Blood and urine cultures were negative, and antibiotics were discontinued after four days. He underwent successful placement of a port for administration of intravenous sodium thiosulfate, which was initiated during the admission. Cinacalcet was started and vitamin D stopped to manage calcium metabolism. His acute kidney injury resolved with hydration, and his blood pressure was controlled on home medications. He was discharged home with plans for outpatient sodium thiosulfate infusions, wound care, and follow-up with dermatology and transplant nephrology.
